extracted.intended_audience: readers of nonprofit journalism and the general public interested in refugee policy and civic issues
extracted.subtask_description: A single-opinion/news commentary drawing historical parallels between WWII Jewish refugees and the Syrian refugee crisis, critiquing political rhetoric and public attitudes toward refugees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize historical parallels when discussing refugee crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and explicitly acknowledge similarities between past refugee crises (e.g., European Jews during World War II) and current events (e.g., Syrian refugees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article links images and experiences—families drowned, confined in railway cars, uncertain futures—and cites comparisons made by writers and outlets (e.g., Ruth McCambridge; The Washington Post). Use historical examples (Anne Frank/Otto Frank attempts to emigrate) to illuminate contemporary policy and public responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fear-based rhetoric and scapegoating
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize on or amplify knee-jerk fears, scapegoating, or ‘not-in-my-backyard’ reactions when discussing refugees or immigration policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticizes politicians who exploit fear (examples: Ben Carson, Donald Trump, Jeb Bush) and parallels 1930s fears of communists/anarchists used against Jews. It calls out magnification of potential dangers into exaggerated risks and warns against political posturing that aims merely to keep people out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base claims and policy positions on documented evidence from credible sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground discussion of atrocities, human-rights conditions, and refugee needs in reports from reputable organizations and commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references documentation by Amnesty International and the United Nations Human Rights Commission and cites a 2014 statement by Paulo Sérgio Pinheiro describing crimes in Syria. Use such authoritative reports to substantiate urgency and moral claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately represent administrative procedures and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to concerns about security or vetting, present accurate information about the screening and resettlement process so public debate is informed rather than alarmist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes President Obama’s point that the refugee vetting system is extensive (18–24 months) and can be so cumbersome it reduces the country’s ability to show compassion. Use precise timelines and procedural facts to counter misleading claims about insufficient vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate for compassionate, timely action rather than delayed responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote policies and public stances that prioritize rescue and assistance promptly rather than waiting for undeniable proof of atrocity before acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article observes that the U.S. only reversed anti-refugee stances in 1944 after full horrors were revealed and references the 1948 Displaced Persons Act as belated remediation. Use historical lessons to argue for earlier humanitarian responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold political actors to higher standards of explanation and moral accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect and require politicians and public figures to understand, explain, and justify their positions on refugees rather than exploiting ignorance or fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece says political candidates should 'know better' and criticizes capitalization on knee-jerk reactions. In commentary or advocacy, demand reasoned explanation and ethical justification for restrictive policies rather than rhetoric.
